item.title: A posteriori estimates for inverse evolutionary problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.26678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The paper is focused on a posteriori error analysis of evolutionary problems, which are ill-posed in the sense of Hadamard. They may have no solutions and respective approximations may be highly unstable. For these problems, the a posteriori error estimation concept applicable to well-posed problems is not valid and requires a significant reformulation. A posteriori estimates of the functional type provide the basis for addressing this issue. They generate computable quantities that estimate the distance between a function (approximate solution to the inverse problem) and exact solution of a "close" well-posed initial boundary value problem associated with the same differential equation. The solution of this close problem exactly satisfies one part of the imposed conditions and the others are satisfied approximately with the accuracy $\eps$. This idea is elaborated for several evolutionary problems generated by the reaction-convection-diffusion equation: backward parabolic problem, problem with non-local time conditions, Cauchy parabolic problem, and parameter(s) identification problem. The estimates derived not only control the accuracy of approximate solutions, but also suggest a unified approach to calculating them numerically.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Zapiski Nauchn. Semin. Steklov Inst. Math. St. Petersburg (POMI), 550(2026), 271--295
item.dc:creator: Sergey Repin

item.title: Pathwise Factorization and Uncertainty Quantification for Impedance Obstacles with Random Boundaries
item.description: arXiv:2611.26761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a factorization method with finite-sample statistical guarantees for two-dimensional acoustic scattering by impedance obstacles whose boundary is random and whose data are finitely many noisy multistatic measurements. In the two-dimensional far-field normalization, the symmetrization must act on a phase-rotated far-field operator; we prove the optical and range identities for every realization of a compact family of uniformly bi-Lipschitz domains, with jointly measurable regularized indicators. A quadrature-weighted finite-sample analysis separates angular approximation, measurement noise, test-vector error, and regularization, and yields a consistency theorem for empirical means and variances, joint in all data parameters. Bounded indicators admit simultaneous confidence bands, a diagonal threshold recovers the probability that a sampling point lies in the random obstacle, and a nested design yields unbiased variance components. Computations use a combined-field integral equation proved invertible at all frequencies, and the finite-grid guarantees are examined in a coverage study against a high-accuracy Monte Carlo reference.
item.dc:creator: George Pelekanos, Koung Hee Leem

item.title: Source Conditions and Sharp Transition Asymptotics for the Factorization Method with Far-Field Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.26778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The factorization method characterizes an obstacle through a range test, but practical implementations replace the associated Picard series by a regularized approximation. This paper studies the resulting regularization bias for inverse acoustic scattering by impedance obstacles. For a disc, we show that every positive-order H\"older source condition fails at each noncentral interior sampling point, whereas logarithmic source conditions hold uniformly on compact interior subsets for every exponent, with explicit constants. At the center, the bias decays linearly with the regularization parameter. We then derive sharp spectral transition asymptotics through the Lambert W function. These asymptotics determine the stabilization rate inside the obstacle, the iterated-logarithmic growth at the boundary, and the divergence outside. They also yield a threshold rule for which the reconstructed disc converges in measure, together with quantitative boundary-location estimates. For general impedance obstacles, we reduce the spectral decay of the symmetrized far-field operator to that of the data-to-pattern operator and obtain two-sided transition bounds in terms of the inradius and any radius larger than the circumradius. For a simply connected obstacle with analytic boundary, positive analytic impedance, and conformal center inside the obstacle, a Faber--Vekua normal form gives the sharp spectral law in terms of logarithmic capacity, with the same leading constant as for the disc. This class includes every convex analytic obstacle. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted spectral transition and illustrate its use in choosing the regularization level. The analytic normal-form result is proved only for a single boundary component.
item.dc:creator: George Pelekanos, Koung Hee Leem

item.title: Recovering from Averages: An Inverse Problem Perspective on Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
item.description: arXiv:2611.26819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate the potential energy surface of atomistic systems from quantum-mechanical reference data and enable molecular simulation at near-ab-initio accuracy at a fraction of the cost. Since they are fitted to total energies and forces, it is not obvious what is estimated: the total energy or the many-body potentials from which it is assembled. Mathematically, this can be formulated as a question whether a function can be recovered from averages of its values over random clusters. We study it for a linear model of fixed correlation order in simplified statistical setting. We show that, in the population limit, the potential is identifiable in a natural weighted Sobolev space, and derive finite-sample recovery guarantees. Numerical experiments for pair, three-body, and four-body models support the theory.
item.dc:creator: Tina Torabi, Cheuk Hin Ho, Christoph Ortner, Ruo Ning Qiu

item.title: A Stochastic Tamed-Regularized Random Batch Method for Uncertain Particle Systems with Singularities
item.description: arXiv:2611.26946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The coefficients of particle systems often exhibit uncertainties due to incomplete knowledge. For particle systems with uncertainties and singularities in the drift and diffusion terms, existing methods may encounter numerical blow-up. In this paper, we propose a novel stochastic tamed-regularized Random Batch (str-RB) method for such uncertain particle systems with singularities. Specifically, since singularities in the diffusion term are more challenging than those in the drift term, building on a tamed scheme, we design an exponential regularization strategy that more effectively mitigates singularities in the diffusion term. This strategy ensures that the stochastic Galerkin (sG) projection coefficients remain finite even when the corresponding integrals for the original singular diffusion coefficient diverge. The sG method is applied to handle the random coefficients, and a random batch approach is then employed to reduce the computational complexity of large-scale simulations. Several theoretical properties of the proposed algorithm are established. Numerical tests demonstrate that the str-RB algorithm exhibits weak convergence, achieves lower errors than major existing methods across singular tests, and remains stable in a wider range of singular regimes. This work provides a robust and accurate approach for uncertain particle systems with singularities, laying a foundation for high-performance solvers in uncertain many-body dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Wenyi Wang, Lei Li, Yiwen Lin

item.title: A linearly decoupled structure-preserving BCFD method for the two-species Keller--Segel chemotaxis system
item.description: arXiv:2611.27004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we develop a fully discrete, linearly decoupled block-centered finite difference scheme for the two-species Keller--Segel chemotaxis system. Based on the Slotboom transformation, the cell-density equations are reformulated into a symmetric form, providing a natural framework for the construction of a structure-preserving discretization. The resulting scheme is shown to unconditionally preserve the positivity of both the cell densities and the chemoattractant concentration, while ensuring exact mass conservation of each cell density and the original energy dissipation. Furthermore, optimal-order error estimates for the proposed scheme are rigorously established through a higher-order consistency analysis. In particular, the cell densities exhibit first-order temporal and second-order spatial convergence in the discrete $L^2$-norm, whereas the chemoattractant concentration achieves the same convergence orders in the discrete $H^1$-norm. Finally, a series of numerical experiments is conducted to verify the theoretical results and demonstrate the reliability of the proposed scheme in simulating the finite-time blow-up phenomenon.
item.dc:creator: Ao Zhang, Bingyin Zhang, Hongfei Fu

item.title: Inverse scattering for the one-dimensional discrete Schr\"odinger operator: a computational perspective
item.description: arXiv:2611.27049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit inverse scattering for the one-dimensional discrete Schr\"odinger operator with compactly supported perturbation. We consider a computational perspective, adapted to the case of a digitally sampled reflection coefficient, to determine the perturbation in the form of a Jacobi matrix, including a computation of the length of the smallest interval supporting the perturbation. A new representation of scattering data in terms of orthogonal polynomials underpins the computational results. A key technical role is played by polynomials on the circle constructed from pairs of successive orthogonal polynomials on the line. The inverse algorithm is demonstrated on numerical examples.
item.dc:creator: Peter C. Gibson, Basant Lal Sharma

item.title: Degree-stratified randomized projection for spectral clustering
item.description: arXiv:2611.27123v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many real-world networks have heavy-tailed degree distributions, in which a few high-degree nodes coexist with many low-degree nodes. Randomized range finders reduce the cost of computing the eigenspace used in spectral clustering, but their random test matrices are constructed independently of the node degrees. We propose degree-stratified randomized projection (DS-RP), which partitions the nodes into dyadic degree strata, distributes a fixed sketch dimension across the strata, and draws an independent local sketch for each stratum. We bound the angle between the sampled range and the target eigenspace and show that the gain comes from the allocation of the sketch dimension rather than from the stratification itself. The bound improves when more sketch dimensions are assigned to the strata on which the target eigenspace is concentrated. For the degree-corrected stochastic block model, we prove that the leverage scores of this eigenspace are proportional to the node degrees, so that the allocation can be determined from the degrees alone. A Rayleigh--Ritz bound that requires no smallness assumption carries the estimate over to the computed spectral embedding. Numerical experiments on synthetic benchmarks and real-world networks show that DS-RP improves the clustering accuracy of standard Gaussian and CountSketch projections at the same sketch dimension and essentially the same computational cost.
item.dc:creator: Junghyun Eom, Youngjin Hwang, Euihyun Kim, Yongseok Jang

item.title: A Higher-Order Algorithm for Solving Time-Fractional Differential Equations via Rational Approximation of z^{\alpha} as a Herglotz-Nevanlinna function
item.description: arXiv:2611.27157v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-Fractional derivatives (TFDs) have been widely used in mathematical modeling of physical phenomena such as anomalous diffusion and memory effects of materials. Traditionally, TFD is handled {either by a direct method which saves almost all the memory and hence computationally expensive or a sum of exponential method (SOE) which decomposes the time domain improper integral into a local term and a history term} {approximated by} a sum of exponential functions. The limitation of the SOE approach is that{ the approximation error of the local term might result in large errors if the unknown function is not smooth enough at $0$ and can lead to over-dissipation of energy.} In this paper, we take a different approach and will focus on the Caputo derivative because the Caputo time derivative of a constant function is 0. We present a simple time-stepping algorithm based on the theory of Stieltjes-Markov functions, a subclass of the Herglotz-Nevanlinna functions. The key is in identifying the Stieltjes-Markov function structure hidden in the Laplace transform of the kernel function. Compared to most of the current methods in literature, the novelty of the results in this paper is manifold. First, no decomposition of integral is needed and our resulting approximation in the time domain contains a Dirac measure with carefully calculated strength, leading to a drastic decrease in the number of exponential functions needed in the approximation. Secondly, the choice of our interpolation points is based on the Mellin's inversion theorem and hence the interpolation error in the transformed domain is explicitly and rigorously linked to the error in the time-domain. {Finally, the resulting system is almost diagonal and hence can be easily sped up by using the Schur complement method.}
item.dc:creator: Miao-jung Yvonne Ou, Gamze Tano\v{g}lu, Jiangming Xie

item.title: Parareal Approximation of Stochastic $L^2$-Boosting
item.description: arXiv:2611.27237v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Parareal approximations of stochastic \(L^2\)-boosting, reusing the learner draws of the sequential algorithm in the fine propagators. We establish mean-square error bounds whose order improves with each correction, characterize the limiting distributions of normalized errors, including non-Gaussian components and the effects of coarse discretization, and derive sufficient conditions for preserving the statistical limit laws and validation-based stopping behavior of the sequential algorithm. Numerical experiments with sample-dependent coordinate and nonlinear residual-fitting learners examine the predicted convergence rates and limiting distributions, while computational benchmarks assess the efficiency of the method relative to sequential implementations.
item.dc:creator: Duc-Quang Bui

item.title: Two-phase visco-elastic FENE-P model: Thermodynamically consistent modeling, sharp interface limit analysis and unconditionally energy stable numerical scheme
item.description: arXiv:2611.27292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Although mathematical modeling and numerical simulations for two-phase Newtonian flows have been extensively studied for many years, relatively little work has focused on developing thermodynamically consistent models for two-phase Non-Newtonian viscoelastic flows, and to the author's best konowledge, no structure-preserving numerical methods have been reported for such models. In this paper, we focus on modeling the two-phase non-Newtonnian visco-elastic FENE-P model based on the energetic variational approach (EnVarA). In the model, a phase-field function is introduced to describe the diffuse interface which satisfies the Cahn-Hilliard (CH) equation. And all the physical variables can be connected smoothly. We conduct a matched asymptotic analysis for the sharp interface limit, which shows the diffuse interface model will converge to the sharp interface model when the interface thickness trends to zero. We then reformulate the model in an equivalent form that facilitates the construction of the numerical scheme. A weakly decoupled scheme is proposed for the resulting FENE-P-CH system, and its unconditional energy stability is proved theoretically. Finally, a series of numerical experiments is conducted to validate the model and assess the performance of the proposed scheme.
item.dc:creator: Yuzhe Qin, Dongdong He

item.title: A fast automatically adaptive integral equation solver for nonlinear two-point boundary value systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.27325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a fast, high-order, automatically adaptive integral-equation solver for nonlinear two-point boundary value systems. The method builds on the fast direct solver for linear second-kind integral equations and completes the mathematical formulation needed for general boundary conditions, including cases in which the simplest background Green's function is singular and cases with genuinely rank-deficient boundary conditions. Nonlinear problems are written as nonlinear second-kind integral equations and are solved by combining this fast adaptive linear solver with Newton iteration and user-specified continuation. In this way the nonlinear solver inherits the full strengths of the linear integral-equation method: a fast direct solver, arbitrary order accuracy, and automatic adaptive resolution with only a small overhead over a solve on the final mesh. The resulting algorithm is particularly effective for problems with localized or multiscale structure, including boundary layers, dense oscillations, transition regions, hypersensitive optimal-control systems, and singular perturbations. The same framework also provides a computational foundation for future studies of bifurcation and solution-branch exploration.
item.dc:creator: Tianze Zhang, Yixuan Ma, Jun Wang

item.title: Karcher means of structured matrices are asymptotically structured: a study via Schatten estimates for the additive Richardson iteration
item.description: arXiv:2611.27335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the present work, we first study the additive Richardson iteration for the Karcher mean of complex Hermitian positive definite (HPD) matrix sequences, by obtaining normalized Schatten estimates independent of the matrix dimension. These estimates are used to prove that Karcher means of structured matrices are asymptotically structured and this is proven for input HPD Toeplitz and generalized locally Toeplitz (GLT) matrix sequences. More precisely, we provide the a.c.s. approximation, which is the key for demonstrating the GLT closure under Schatten spectral bounds, and the GLT conclusion can be extended to matrix sequences with symbols that are positive definite almost everywhere. Ad hoc numerical experiments illustrate the spectral distribution consequences of these results and few related computational advantages. Concluding remarks and open problems are provided in the final section.
item.dc:creator: Samuele Ferri, Valerio Loi, Stefano Serra-Capizzano, Giacomo Tento

item.title: A 3D PINN-Based Framework for Patient-Specific Pulmonary Hemodynamics Using Windkessel Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.27351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cardiovascular fluid dynamics modeling relies heavily on mesh-based numerical methods such as Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). While accurate, these methods entail significant computational costs and complex meshing workflows that limit their translation to clinical practice. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are a promising meshless alternative that embeds the governing equations directly into neural network training. In this work, we propose a PINN framework for pulsatile blood flow in patient-specific geometries with dynamic lumped-parameter Windkessel (RCR) outlet conditions representing distal vascular impedance. Coupling the Windkessel ODE to a 3D network raises two difficulties: the ODE alone does not fix the pressure level, and the local pressure variations that drive the flow are orders of magnitude smaller than the basal pressure imposed by the outlet. We address them by decomposing pressure into a time-dependent basal part and a spatially varying part, an initial condition and gauge for the Windkessel equation, a global mass-balance constraint, and a periodic Fourier embedding of time. Validated on 2D canonical channels (steady and pulsatile, with and without RCR outlet), the framework is then applied to a patient-specific right pulmonary artery, reproducing outlet flow, mean pressure, and the velocity and dynamic pressure fields with errors on the order of the data resolution. Finally, we solve the inverse problem of identifying the three Windkessel parameters of the outlet from synthetic data, recovering them with errors of about 0.3% from deliberately wrong initial values. Residual biases in the local pressure field and the need to test robustness to noisy clinical data remain open, but the results support PINNs as complementary tools for meshless hemodynamics and patient-specific digital twins.
item.dc:creator: Celia Taboada, Luis Nu\~nez, Ang\'elica Casero, Pedro Navas

item.title: Structure-Preserving Model Reduction of Metriplectic Systems via Oblique Projections and Block Structure
item.description: arXiv:2611.27393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metriplectic systems combine conservative and dissipative dynamics and are characterized by energy conservation and entropy production. The degeneracy conditions underlying these properties are generally not preserved by standard projection-based model order reduction. We develop two structure-preserving reduction strategies. The first enforces degeneracy conditions through oblique projections and combines gradient-preserving and matrix empirical interpolation for hyper-reduction. The second constructs reduced bases adapted to available operator block structure, preserving degeneracy without online oblique corrections. We establish sufficient conditions for preserving the Jacobi identity and derive a priori error estimates. Numerical tests on benchmark problems demonstrate accuracy, thermodynamic consistency, and computational efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Benvenuti, Cecilia Pagliantini

item.title: Do DeepONet Trunk-Basis Preconditioners Need Training?
item.description: arXiv:2611.27582v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trunk-basis (TB) preconditioners build the coarse space of a two-level Schwarz preconditioner from the trunk functions of a trained deep operator network (DeepONet), restricted to subdomains. Their effectiveness has been attributed to spectral bias since networks learn low frequencies first, complementing a smoother that removes the high-frequency error. Spectral bias, however, is a property of training, whereas a randomly initialized trunk with a smooth activation is already smooth. We therefore ask whether TB preconditioners need training. In one dimension, we prove that on each subdomain the span of untrained trunk functions is close to the space of low-degree polynomials under suitable nondegeneracy assumptions. Numerically, for the Poisson equation and three-dimensional linear elasticity with constant coefficients, untrained TB and piecewise polynomial coarse spaces of equal dimension yield close conjugate gradient iteration counts, while training with the standard \(\ell^2\) loss sometimes increases them. Training can improve iteration counts when high-contrast coefficients make the low-energy modes non-smooth, and if the loss measures the error in the energy norm. For the Poisson equation with contrast \(10^5\), energy-trained TB coarse spaces need fewer iterations than piecewise polynomials of equal dimension, whereas \(\ell^2\)-trained ones do not. For a topology-optimized elastic cantilever with contrast \(10^6\), the energy-trained TB space enriched with the rigid-body modes gives the fewest iterations at larger coarse dimensions. This suggests that for neural operator-based hybrid solvers, a network's inductive bias and training objective should match the solver.
item.dc:creator: Jaemin Oh, Jerome Darbon, George Em Karniadakis

item.title: Convex Structure-Preserving EDMD: Passive Koopman Matrices as $Q$-Contractions
item.description: arXiv:2611.27730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) approximates the Koopman operator using a matrix based on a finite set of observables. However, the least-squares matrix of a port-Hamiltonian (pH) system is generally neither passive nor invariant-preserving. We demonstrate that the implicit midpoint discretization of a lifted pH model precisely preserves energy balance, passivity, and all linear Casimirs for every step size. For a fixed storage metric $Q$, the resulting Koopman matrices are the Cayley transforms of $(J-R)Q$, where $J$ is skew-symmetric and $R$ is positive semidefinite. This set does not depend on the step size and is the closure of all Q-contractions. This set is LMI-representable; therefore, structure-preserving EDMD, including ports through a discrete-time Kalman-Yakubovich-Popov condition and Casimirs through affine constraints, is a semidefinite program. The constrained estimate is a projection of the unconstrained estimate in the data-weighted norm and cannot increase estimation error when the population target is pH-compatible. For every $Q$-contraction, a certified bound on the lifted prediction error grows linearly at most in time, whereas it grows geometrically for unconstrained models with Q-gain above one. Benchmarks on a damped pendulum and a damped rigid body demonstrate that constrained models never generate energy and that imposed Casimirs are maintained with solver accuracy (approximately $10^{-8}$). In contrast, EDMD may diverge or lose the Casimir with noisy data. The benchmarks also demonstrate that when $Q$ is the physical energy, the constrained models are less accurate than EDMD and can exhibit significant structural bias.
item.dc:creator: Matthias Ehrhardt, Achraf Zinihi

item.title: Data-Adaptive Entropy-Based Moment Reduction for Vlasov-Poisson-Dougherty Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.27904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a data-adaptive entropy-based moment method for the Vlasov-Poisson-Dougherty system with self-consistent temperature. A positive exponential representation augments the physical moments with data-adapted velocity functions. The collision guarantees are independent of basis construction: for every fixed basis satisfying the stated rank condition, the reduced collision step is uniquely solvable, positive, locally conservative and entropy-dissipative. These guarantees persist under a positive empirical cubature method (ECM), enabling structure-preserving collision hyper-reduction. We construct the basis by proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), fit it with a neural network and post-train it through the reduced dynamics. In two-stream relaxation, sustained heating and drive switching, one fixed post-trained basis with thirteen variables per cell attains space-time distribution errors below 0.25% against same-grid full-order solutions. Post-training lowers this error relative to the neural fit in all three tests and to POD in the two driven tests. With full-grid MUSCL retained, matched drive-switching timings give 1.36-2.89-fold online speedups over the full-order solver using 128-1024 velocity nodes.
item.dc:creator: Shiheng Zhang, Jiahao Zhang, Guang Lin

item.title: A Coats-Based Formulation for Multiphase Reactive Transport Accounting for Aqueous Phase Disappearance
item.description: arXiv:2611.27930v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As part of the energy transition, underground hydrogen (H2) storage in porous media has emerged as an alternative solution for large-scale energy storage to salt caverns. Assessing the feasibility of such systems and ensuring their operation requires accurate modeling of the geochemical processes that may alter the composition of the stored gas. This results in a highly nonlinear coupled system of partial differential equations, ordinary differential equations, and algebraic constraints, calling for robust and specialized numerical strategies. In this work, we adopt a Globally Implicit Approach (GIA), as sequential solution algorithms are known to introduce splitting errors due to the decoupling of flow and geochemical processes. In addition, most splitting-based methods implicitly assume the persistent presence of the liquid phase, an assumption that may be violated during gas injection or withdrawal owing to aqueous phase vaporization and mineral precipitation in the vicinity of wells. We extend Coats' formulation to multiphase reactive transport with a rigorous and fully implicit management of aqueous phase disappearance and reappearance. The proposed approach introduces new molar concentration unknowns for basis species that track the re-appearance of the aqueous phase and guarantee the nonsingularity of the Jacobian matrix. Additionally, the appearance of the liquid phase is managed using a multiphase flash calculation algorithm. The proposed algorithm is validated against the CO2 storage benchmark problems. Finally, the approach is applied to an underground H2 storage in an aquifer under cyclic injection and withdrawal conditions.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Jacumin, Roland Masson, Laurent Jeannin, Arthur Dartois

item.title: Convergence of a finite element Chorin projection method for the stochastic Navier--Stokes equations
item.description: arXiv:2611.27969v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analyze a fully discrete finite element projection method for the stochastic incompressible Navier--Stokes equations with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and multiplicative noise. We show solvability and uniform moment estimates for the intermediate and the corrected velocity approximations under the assumption that the initial data is square-integrable and divergence free, and that the deterministic forcing term is bounded in $L^{q}(0,T;H^{-1}(D))$ for a sufficiently large $q$. Under standard stability and approximation assumptions on the finite element spaces and a coupling condition on the spatial and temporal discretization parameters, we prove convergence of a subsequence to a martingale solution of the stochastic Navier--Stokes equations. The analysis combines the complementary spatial and temporal estimates of the predicted and the corrected velocity approximations and uses the numerical dissipation to identify their common limit. We establish tightness of the piecewise constant temporal interpolations of the velocity field approximations using Aldous' criterion combined with the uniform discrete moment estimates. The convergence result holds in two and three space dimensions as it does not rely on any additional regularity of the limiting martingale solution beyond the one naturally available from the energy inequality. Finally, we demonstrate the performance of the scheme in numerical experiments in two space dimensions for smooth and vortex sheet initial data.
item.dc:creator: Franziska Weber

item.title: A boundary integral equation solver for capsule suspensions
item.description: arXiv:2611.26795v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deformable capsules serve as models for biological cells, such as red blood cells, as well as for synthetic capsules in biomedical and industrial applications. In this work, we introduce a framework for fast and robust simulation of deformable capsules in three-dimensional Stokes flow, both in unbounded domains and in pipe-confined geometries. We solve the Stokes equations using a boundary integral formulation, employing a partition-of-unity discretization for the capsule membrane and the trapezoidal rule with regularization to handle the singular quadrature. Dense periodic interactions are evaluated via a fast Ewald summation scheme, achieving $O(N \log N)$ complexity for $N$ grid points. The interfacial forces on the capsule membrane are modeled using the Skalak constitutive law. We carry out a spectral analysis of this model for small perturbations of a spherical capsule, which indicates that the relaxation dynamics are intrinsically stable. However, the nonlinear character of the Skalak model induces aliasing errors that can compromise numerical stability. To address this when needed, we perform de-aliasing through upsampling and spectral filtering, and we derive guidelines for choosing appropriate filter parameters, thereby stabilizing the method. We investigate the stability and convergence behavior of the resulting scheme and conduct simulations of long-time dynamics, focusing on the relaxation of unconfined capsules and the lateral migration of pipe-confined capsules under various flow conditions.
item.dc:creator: Joar Bagge, Ziyu Du, George Biros

item.title: Optimized solver algorithms for computing $\mathrm{Tr}(A^{-1})$
item.description: arXiv:2611.26854v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Estimating the trace of the inverse of a large quark matrix is a longstanding problem in lattice QCD. The standard approach is Hutchinson's method, which uses random noise vectors to estimate the trace to a desired statistical tolerance. Each noise vector $b$ requires solving a system of linear equations $Ax = b$. In this work, we introduce a new class of Krylov solvers for this task, called Twin methods. Twin methods generate the Krylov polynomial once then reuse it on all other right-hand sides. This reduces the number of basic linear algebra operations in the algorithm and therefore lowers the trace computation time. We apply the Twin approach to BiCG and BiCGStab and test them on lattice QCD matrices of varying size and in a range of computing contexts. We also present a more economical estimation of $\mathrm{Tr}(A^{-1})$ which implements a polynomial approximation of $A^{-1}$ and a singular value deflation. In this scheme, the solvers are applied to only a few noise vectors, and the remainder are treated by the polynomial and the deflation. In our tests, the polynomial approximation combined with the deflation yield a 17-fold speedup in the time required to compute the trace over standard Hutchinson's method.
item.dc:creator: Benjamin Luke, Sudip Shiwakoti, Shayan Nadeem, Ronald Morgan, Walter Wilcox

item.title: Semigroup Hessian Estimates for Underdamped Langevin Dynamics
item.description:
arXiv:2611.26930v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For the semigroup $e^{t\mathcal L}$ of the underdamped Langevin dynamics, we bound the Hessian $
abla^2(e^{t\mathcal L}f)$ when $
abla f$ is uniformly bounded. When the potential is strongly convex outside a ball and has bounded second and third derivatives, and the damping rate is above an explicit threshold, the bounds on $
abla^2(e^{t\mathcal L}f)$ decay exponentially in time with constants free of the dimension. The proof combines the Wasserstein contraction of the dynamics with a Bismut--Elworthy--Li formula for the degenerate noise. As an application, we prove the uniform-in-time error of the stochastic gradient UBU integrator, with an explicit coefficient of the numerical bias in the step size, proportional to the covariance of the stochastic gradient noise.
item.dc:creator: Xuda Ye, Zhihan Zhang

item.title: Spectral Estimation with Deformed Decompression
item.description: arXiv:2611.26945v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sample covariance matrices are fundamental objects in machine learning and statistics, with valuable information encoded into their eigenvalues. When treating modern problems, the scale of these matrices can become prohibitive for tractable computation. This creates a critical need for "spectral decompression": a method for inferring the eigenspectrum of a very large-scale model using only information from its smaller realizations. Existing methods fall into two main categories: those relying on spectral inversion; and those that rely on Free Decompression techniques. On the one hand, spectral inversion is a fundamentally ill-posed problem that is notoriously unstable, often failing to yield reliable results in finite-size settings. On the other hand, while Free Decompression was recently proposed to address this scaling, its reliance on the Nica-Speicher framework restricts its use to unitarily invariant ensembles, a symmetry condition that subsampled covariance matrices fail to satisfy. In this work, we introduce Deformed Decompression (DD), a novel framework for the stable, forward-extrapolation of spectral densities. By leveraging properties of the companion matrix, DD recasts the spectral decompression problem as a directed evolution of the Stieltjes transform of the companion matrix. This approach bypasses the instabilities of traditional inversion and provides a robust methodology for scaling covariance matrices and even their generalized variants (including Hessian matrices) that lack unitary invariance. We demonstrate the utility of our framework through experiments on a variety of random matrix examples, showing that DD successfully captures the complex spectral signatures of large-scale systems.
item.dc:creator: Siavash Ameli, Chris van der Heide, Liam Hodgkinson, Michael W. Mahoney

item.title: On the convergence of greedy algorithms in one-dimensional Wasserstein space
item.description: arXiv:2611.27086v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the convergence of the greedy algorithm for approximating a compact set by barycenters in metric spaces, in particular in the space of one-dimensional measures endowed with the 2-Wasserstein distance. To this end, we compare several metric $N$-widths, which measure the best error achievable with $N$-point barycenters, using either classical barycenters having nonnegative weights or signed barycenters, with weights of arbitrary sign summing to one. For the analysis we exploit that quantile functions embed the one-dimensional 2-Wasserstein space isometrically into a convex cone of $L^2(0,1)$, and barycenter sets correspond to nonlinear projections of convex or affine hulls. We prove, both in the algebraic and exponential case, that the convergence rate of the greedy algorithm using signed barycenters matches the one of the metric $N$-width defined with classical barycenters. We provide counterexamples showing that this fails for the other combinations.
item.dc:creator: Genevi\`eve Dusson, Carlo Marcati, Maximilian Penka

item.title: A Validation-Driven Bilevel Optimization Method for Mesh-Free PDE Solvers and Its Error Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.27347v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Mesh-free partial differential equation (PDE) solvers construct discrete systems from residuals at sampled points. These solvers fit coefficients in a parameterized trial representation and select solver-design parameters governing the representation, training-residual weighting, and regularization. These parameters strongly affect solution accuracy, yet existing selection strategies are largely tailored to particular solver classes. To address this limitation, we formulate a unified validation-driven bilevel optimization framework applicable across different solver classes, in which the lower level fits coefficients using training collocation residuals, while the upper level selects solver-design parameters using held-out validation residuals. For nonlinear PDEs, however, solving the nonlinear lower-level problem to high accuracy is costly, while the adjoint system is typically ill-conditioned and indefinite. To address this issue, we propose an efficient implicit hypergradient method that approximates the lower-level response using finite, warm-started damped Gauss-Newton (GN) updates. For the adjoint solve, we use the damped GN matrix to compute an initial adjoint and to precondition a finite number of minimum residual iterations. To quantify the errors introduced by these approximations, we derive local hypergradient error bounds that separate the contributions of the finite lower-level solve, adjoint damping, and the final adjoint residual. Combining this analysis with validation sampling bounds and residual stability, we relate validation residuals to PDE solution accuracy and establish error bounds for the computed PDE solution. Numerical experiments on several nonlinear PDEs, including a high-dimensional problem, demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method across Kansa, random feature and extreme learning machine, and physics-informed neural network solvers.
item.dc:creator: Yongcun Song, Shangzhi Zeng, Jin Zhang, Lvgang Zhang

item.title: Linear Convergence of Adaptive Accelerated Gradient Methods: A Unified Framework
item.description: arXiv:2611.27366v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We establish a unified Lyapunov framework for adaptive accelerated gradient methods on smooth, strongly convex objectives. Conditions on local curvature, stepsize ratios, and coefficient variation ensure eventual linear convergence without assuming stepsize convergence. We verify these conditions for specified AdaNAG-G, smooth unconstrained AC-FGM, and AdaAGM policies and use them to design VC-FG and CC-FG. The verified adaptive main iterations require neither global smoothness nor strong-convexity parameters and avoid restart and backtracking. The framework also sharpens a fixed-step FISTA/NAG-type bound. Experiments on four smooth, strongly convex problem families illustrate complementary performance of the new methods.
item.dc:creator: Weihe Zhang, Ming Yan

item.title: Structure-preserving compression of Matrix Product States
item.description: arXiv:2611.27408v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Matrix product state time evolution relies on compression to control the growth of bond dimensions, but compression can break the conservation laws of the equation being solved. A truncation is not the flow of a Hermitian generator, so even a small truncation error can violate exact algebraic identities of the Schr\"odinger equation. For any matrix product state integrator that leaves the state in canonical form with an orthogonality center, a scalar correction restores an admissible global invariant after compression whenever the resulting scalar quadratic constraint equation admits a real root, without enlarging any bond dimension. Rank-preserving recovery searches other canonical centers when that correction fails. The geometry of the low-rank manifold provides sufficient conditions for conservation by the fixed-rank projected flow and bounds what corrections within a frozen center frame can achieve. Numerical experiments demonstrate that recovery can be required even along accurate truncated trajectories.
item.dc:creator: Pouriya Ghadimi, Maximilian Fr\"ohlich, Aaron Sander, Martin Eigel, Richard M. Milbradt

item.title: Consensus of Consensus: Decentralized Consensus-Based Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2611.27433v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose and analyze a decentralized variant of Consensus-Based Optimization (CBO) for the global minimization of continuous, possibly non-convex functions accessible only through a stochastic, possibly biased, zeroth-order oracle with bounded mean-squared error. The agents are split among $N$ units of an undirected communication network. Each unit evolves its swarm of $M$ agents towards a local tracking variable, which follows the network average of the local consensus points through one round of neighbour-to-neighbour communication via a doubly stochastic mixing matrix, without any central coordinator. We show that, under an explicit condition linking the drift and diffusion parameters to $M$, all agents reach consensus almost surely, at an exponential mean-square rate governed by the spectrum of the mixing matrix. Using a finite-agent quantitative Laplace principle, we prove that, for large $\alpha$ and provided some agent visits a neighbourhood of the global minimizer with sufficient probability, the expected mean-squared distance of the swarm from the minimizer falls below any tolerance within an explicit number of iterations, at a rate that deteriorates for poorly connected networks. We verify this hitting assumption for a simplified dynamics. Experiments on benchmarks up to dimension $d=1000$, with stochastic objectives, and on a federated learning task demonstrate the method's effectiveness.
item.dc:creator: Stefania Bellavia, Massimo Fornasier, Greta Malaspina, Tim Roith

item.title: Scattering by two parallel semi--infinite arrays of sound--soft scatterers
item.description: arXiv:2611.27481v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This article considers the scattering of an acoustic wave by two identical semi--infinite arrays of point scatterers which are positioned parallel to one another. The resulting system of scattering coefficients is formulated as a pair of coupled discrete Wiener--Hopf equations with a full $2\times2$ matrix kernel composed of two scalar kernel functions that represent interaction within the selected array and between the two arrays. Exploiting the symmetry of the two arrays, we introduce symmetric and antisymmetric components of the scattering coefficients, which decouple the matrix Wiener--Hopf system into two independent scalar problems with kernels given by the sum and difference of the two original kernel functions. The scalar Wiener--Hopf equations are then solved using the Wiener--Hopf technique in a very similar way to what has previously been used to solve the semi--infinite array problem. The original definitions of the two scalar kernels are represented by a lattice sum and practical evaluation techniques are discussed. Comparisons with previous work are also critically discussed. The resulting formulation provides an exact analytical solution to a coupled semi--infinite array problem and illustrates how symmetry can reduce a discrete matrix Wiener--Hopf problem to two scalar problems.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Nethercote

item.title: Generalized Markov numbers and plane lattices
item.description: arXiv:2611.27627v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We give new explicit constructions of lattice rules in the two-dimensional square and torus. It is well-known that uniformly distributed lattices (in the sense of low-discrepancy) arise from continued fractions with bounded partial denominators. We demonstrate how integers solutions of the generalized Markov equation $x^2+y^2+z^2 = kxyz-k+3$ give rise to such lattices.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Nagel, Friedrich Pillichshammer

item.title: Energy-preserving Bayesian model reduction: closed-form structured posteriors and probabilistic stability certificates for quadratic operator inference
item.description: arXiv:2611.27794v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bayesian operator inference learns reduced-order models (ROMs) with polynomial structure from state data and returns a closed-form Gaussian posterior over the reduced operators. That posterior is unconstrained, so it gives positive probability to operators with unbounded dynamics, and current practice controls this only through finite-horizon simulation tests on a few samples. We show that energy preservation of the quadratic operator is a set of linear equality constraints, which can be imposed exactly inside the Bayesian formulation without losing the closed form. In particular, the constrained posterior follows from one Kalman-type update of the unconstrained one, and its samples are obtained exactly, by the same correction applied to unconstrained draws. Under this structure, global boundedness for all initial conditions and bounded inputs reduces to a linear matrix condition on the symmetric part of the linear operator. The simulation test is then replaced by a probabilistic stability certificate: the posterior probability that the ROM is globally bounded, estimated with exact confidence bounds; the posterior restricted to certified models is then sampled exactly by rejection. For energy-conserving systems, the linear part can be constrained to be skew-symmetric as well: every draw then grows at most linearly in time, and conserves energy exactly when unforced. On a forced viscous Burgers' equation, the Korteweg-de Vries equation and a two-dimensional viscous Burgers' equation, every sample of the constrained posterior integrates to a bounded trajectory, where up to all unconstrained draws diverge, and beyond the observation window the former is also the more accurate of the two.
item.dc:creator: Jo\~ao Victor Galv\~ao da Mata, Mengwu Guo

item.title: Tackling Many-Body Coulomb Singularity by Randomization
item.description: arXiv:2611.27851v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many-body Coulomb dynamics is central to quantum chemistry and molecular simulation, yet the Coulomb singularity undermines both the standard error analysis and performance of product formulas. Even for the simple hydrogen ground state, the celebrated Trotter formulas converge more slowly than their nominal order, and going to higher order does not help. Randomization by itself does not resolve this. We show that conventional qDRIFT suffers the same loss of accuracy, and that for general initial states, the errors of both Trotter formulas and qDRIFT can decrease more slowly than any power of the number of time steps (logarithmically). To overcome these limitations, we introduce supersmoothing qDRIFT, a randomized product formula that turns a physical property of free particle propagation into an algorithmic resource. Our algorithm achieves an error bound that decreases linearly with the time step, uniformly over \textit{all} initial states and without any smoothness or energy assumptions. Combined with spatial discretization analysis, the resulting end-to-end gate count improves on those of qubitization and high-order Trotter formulas applied directly to the discretized Hamiltonian, despite first-order convergence in time. This work demonstrates new ways of utilizing continuum dynamics to achieve algorithmic advantage.
item.dc:creator: Di Fang, Wook Yoon

item.title: A Certified Reduced Basis Method for Linear Parametrized Parabolic Optimal Control Problems in Space-Time Formulation
item.description: arXiv:2103.00460v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we propose to efficiently solve time dependent parametrized optimal control problems governed by parabolic partial differential equations through the certified reduced basis method. In particular, we will exploit an error estimator procedure, based on easy-to-compute quantities which guarantees a rigorous and efficient bound for the error of the involved variables. First, we propose analyzing the problem at hand, proving its well-posedness thanks to Ne\v cas - Babu\v ska theory in a space-time formulation. Then, we derive error estimators to apply a Greedy method during the offline stage, to perform, during the online stage, a Galerkin projection onto a low-dimensional space spanned by properly chosen high-fidelity solutions. We tested the error estimators on two model problems governed by a Graetz flow with physical and geometrical parametrization. The results have been compared to a previously proposed bound, based on the exact computation of the Babu\v ska inf-sup constant, in terms of reliability and computational costs. We remark that our findings still hold in the steady setting, and we also propose a brief insight for this simpler formulation.
item.dc:creator: Maria Strazzullo, Francesco Ballarin, Gianluigi Rozza

item.title: H(curl)-based approximation of the Stokes problem with slip boundary conditions
item.description: arXiv:2407.13353v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reformulating the incompressible Stokes equations with the velocity sought in H(curl) has recently emerged as a promising approach for the design of helicity-preserving schemes in magnetohydrodynamics and pressure-robust finite element methods on polygonal meshes. A key challenge in this setting, however, is the treatment of Navier slip boundary conditions. In this paper, we overcome this difficulty by recasting the slip condition as a Robin boundary condition and proving well-posedness (up to a finite-dimensional kernel) of the resulting continuous problem. We further identify the geometric and regularity assumptions on the domain and the exact solution under which the classical Stokes solution is recovered. Finally, we study a finite element Galerkin discretization, establishing stability and a priori error estimates. Numerical experiments validate the optimal convergence rates predicted by the theory.
item.dc:creator: Wietse M. Boon, Ralf Hiptmair, Wouter Tonnon, Enrico Zampa

item.title: A polytopal discontinuous Galerkin method for the pseudo-stress formulation of the unsteady Stokes problem
item.description: arXiv:2408.08760v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This work aims to construct and analyze a discontinuous Galerkin method on polytopal grids (PolydG) to solve the pseudo-stress formulation of the unsteady Stokes problem. The pseudo-stress variable is introduced due to the growing interest in non-Newtonian flows and coupled interface problems, where stress assumes a fundamental role. The space-time discretization of the problem is achieved by combining the PolydG approach with the implicit theta-method time integration scheme. For both the semi- and fully-discrete problems we present a detailed stability analysis. Moreover, we derive convergence estimates for the fully discrete space-time discretization. A set of verification tests is presented to verify the theoretical estimates and the application of the method to cases of engineering interest.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering, 447:118404 (2025)
item.dc:creator: Paola F. Antonietti, Michele Botti, Alessandra Cancrini, Ilario Mazzieri

item.title: Stable Nonlinear Dynamical Approximation with Dynamical Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2505.11938v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a nonlinear dynamical approximation method for time-dependent Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). The approach makes use of parametrized decoder functions, and provides a general, and principled way of understanding and analyzing stability and accuracy of nonlinear dynamical approximations. The parameters of these functions are evolved in time by means of projections on finite dimensional subspaces of an ambient Hilbert space related to the PDE evolution. For practical computations of these projections, one usually needs to sample. We propose a dynamical sampling strategy which comes with stability guarantees, while keeping a low numerical complexity. We show the effectiveness of the method on several examples in moderate spatial dimension.
item.dc:creator: Daan Bon, Benjamin Caris, Olga Mula

item.title: A residual driven multiscale method for Darcy's flow in perforated domains
item.description: arXiv:2506.23093v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we present a residual-driven multiscale method for simulating Darcy flow in perforated domains, where complex geometries and highly heterogeneous permeability make direct simulations computationally expensive. To address this, we introduce a velocity elimination technique that reformulates the mixed velocity-pressure system into a pressure-only formulation, significantly reducing complexity by focusing on the dominant pressure variable. Our method is developed within the Generalized Multiscale Finite Element Method (GMsFEM) framework. For each coarse block, we construct offline basis functions from local spectral problems that capture key geometric and physical features. Online basis functions are then adaptively enriched using residuals, allowing the method to incorporate global effects such as source terms and boundary conditions, thereby improving accuracy. We provide detailed error analysis demonstrating how the offline and online spaces contribute to the accuracy and efficiency of the solution. Numerical experiments confirm the method's effectiveness, showing substantial reductions in computational cost while maintaining high accuracy, particularly through adaptive online enrichment. These results highlight the method's potential for efficient and accurate simulation of Darcy flow in complex, heterogeneous perforated domains.
item.dc:creator: Wei Xie, Shubin Fu, Yin Yang, Yunqing Huang

item.title: Numerical Analysis of 2D Stochastic Navier--Stokes Equations with Transport Noise: Regularity and Spatial Semidiscretization
item.description: arXiv:2512.03483v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper establishes a strong convergence rate for the spatial finite element discretization of a two-dimensional stochastic Navier--Stokes system with transport noise and no-slip boundary conditions on a convex polygonal domain. The main challenge arises from the lack of spatial $D(A)$-regularity of the solutio (where $A$ is the Stokes operator), which prevents the direct applicability of standard error analysis techniques. Under a smallness assumption on the transport noise, for a MINI-element spatial semidiscretization, we establish a strong convergence rate of order $h^{\varrho} \log\big(1 + \frac{1}{h}\big)$, where $\varrho \in (0,1/2)$.
item.dc:creator: Binjie Li, Qin Zhou

item.title: A unified perspective of Gaussian process approximation for differential equations
item.description: arXiv:2607.06292v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The use of Gaussian processes for approximating differential equations has expanded rapidly, leading to a growing, diverse, and fragmented body of numerical methods. We present a unified Bayesian perspective that places these techniques within a common probabilistic framework, based on a derivative matching interpretation for incorporating differential equation constraints into likelihood. This unified perspective supports both parameter estimation and solution approximation, and shows how a range of existing methods can be understood within it. This work aims to consolidate current developments and provide a foundation for future research.
item.dc:creator: Mengwu Guo

item.title: Convergence and acceleration of a nonlinear fixed-point iteration for computing the Fitness Centrality of general graphs
item.description: arXiv:2608.28634v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We establish the global convergence of the (non-homogeneous) Fitness Centrality algorithm for general graphs, deriving an explicit convergence bound for the corresponding fixed-point iteration. From the computational point of view, we show how the convergence can be dramatically improved by Anderson acceleration and by switching to Newton's method once a sufficiently good approximation to the fixed point has been found. The efficacy of this strategy is illustrated by numerical experiments on different types of graphs.
item.dc:creator: Nikita Deniskin, Michele Benzi

item.title: Interval Inverse Inequalities for Multiscale Kernel Primitives with Positive Exponential Spectra
item.description: arXiv:2610.07612v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Inverse inequalities are fundamental for controlling derivative growth and ensuring sampling stability in kernel-based approximation. Extending whole-space and single-scale estimates to multiscale analytic spaces on bounded intervals requires uniform control of boundary truncation and cross-scale cancellation. We establish unweighted $L^2(0,1)$ inverse inequalities of sharp scaling order $h_*^{-1}$ for trial spaces spanned by affine functions and multiscale primitives of kernels with positive exponential spectra, where $h_*$ denotes the finest scale. Under geometric scale separation and within-scale center separation, the inverse constant depends only on the kernel and separation parameters; it is independent of the number of scales and centers, allowing centers at the endpoints and arbitrary cross-scale center coincidences. To prove the bound, we combine an exterior Gram decomposition with endpoint-distance weights to establish configuration-uniform Riesz bounds for normalized high-order derivatives of order $q$, whose lower constant approaches the optimal limit $1/2$. A synthesis-operator perturbation argument and parameterized interval interpolation then yield the first-order estimate. Two-center constructions confirm sharpness in both the scaling order $h_*^{-1}$ and the $q^{-1/2}$ asymptotic deficit from $1/2$ as $q \to \infty$. An application to deterministic least-squares sampling is derived, and numerical experiments on boundary-layer asymptotics, multiscale Gram spectra, sharp inverse constants, and midpoint sampling illustrate the theory.
item.dc:creator: Chengming Li, Qiming Wang

item.title: Numerical reconstruction of polygonal obstacles by diffracted waves
item.description: arXiv:2610.31271v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a numerical method for recovering rigid polygonal obstacles in two dimensions, based on the diffraction-based inverse scattering theory of Bao, Chen, Lu, and Xiong. A single pulse is emitted from a point source, and the resulting wave field is measured on a receiver curve. After isolating the diffracted signals, we recover the visible vertices from arrival times and the corner orientations and opening angles from amplitudes. The use of amplitude information permits local reconstruction in the reflection shadow, where reflected waves do not reach the receiver. The amplitudes also determine the direction of a shadowed edge adjacent to a visible vertex, enabling local non-line-of-sight imaging. Numerical experiments for a convex corner, a concave corner, a triangle, a pentagon, and a star-shaped obstacle confirm that the visible portion of the boundary can be recovered stably from diffracted signals. A further convex-corner test with additive noise at level $0.2\%$ on the single arc $L_{1}$ confirms that the tip and opening remain recoverable.
item.dc:creator: Xi Chen, Kuangmiao Xiong, Boxi Xu

item.title: On the Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for multi-layer ResNets in the mean-field regime
item.description: arXiv:2110.02926v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Finding the optimal configuration of parameters in ResNet is a nonconvex minimization problem, but first-order methods often find the global optimum when the network is overparameterized and the training algorithm is run for sufficiently many iterations. We study this phenomenon in the mean-field regime, where the network can be described approximately by an ordinary integral equation (OIE) and the training process of ResNet becomes a gradient-flow partial differential equation (PDE). Under the condition that the activation function is $2$-homogeneous or partially $1$-homogeneous, we show that this gradient-flow PDE converges to the global minimum. This result suggests that if the ResNet is sufficiently large, first-order optimization methods can find global minimizers that fit the training data as well. Further, by controlling the generalization error, we prove that the gradient-flow PDE is stable with respect to its cost function, implying that a finite-sized but sufficiently large dataset drawn from the underlying data distribution can exhibit the properties of the continuous limit. We give lower bounds on the depth and width of the network for the gradient-flow approximation to hold. We also lower-bound the size of the training data set needed to attain accurate approximation.
item.dc:creator: Zhiyan Ding, Shi Chen, Qin Li, Stephen Wright

item.title: Adaptive Lipschitz-Free Proximal Gradient Methods for Stochastic Composite Nonconvex Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2502.21099v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose {\sf ALFPG}, an Adaptive Lipschitz-Free Proximal Gradient framework for stochastic composite nonconvex minimization. It adapts stepsizes from the optimization trajectory without requiring smoothness constants or line search. For finite-sum problems, {\sf ALFPG-FS} combines coordinate-wise stepsizes, Nesterov extrapolation, and a SPIDER estimator; {\sf ALFPG-D} is its full-batch specialization. Under component-wise smoothness, bounded sublevel sets, and separate lower bounds on $f$ and $h$, {\sf ALFPG-FS} achieves expected $\epsilon$-stationarity with $\mathcal O(N+\sqrt N \epsilon^{-2})$ component-gradient evaluations. For expectation problems, we develop {\sf ALFPG-MVR1} and {\sf ALFPG-MVR2} (MVR: Momentum-based Variance Reduction). Both use one fresh sample per iteration. MVR1 uses one stochastic-gradient evaluation; MVR2 uses at most two evaluations at different points with the same sample. MVR1 requires smoothness of the expected loss; MVR2 additionally requires uniformly smooth sample losses. When the regularizer is convex or Lipschitz continuous on its effective domain and stochastic gradients are almost surely bounded, both methods achieve expected $\epsilon$-stationarity using $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\sigma^2\epsilon^{-4}+\epsilon^{-2})$ and $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\sigma\epsilon^{-3}+\epsilon^{-2})$ stochastic-gradient evaluations, respectively. Here, $N$ is the number of component functions, $\sigma^2$ bounds the gradient noise variance, and $\widetilde{\mathcal O}$ hides polylogarithmic factors. Neither expectation variant requires prior knowledge of $\sigma$, and both recover $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\epsilon^{-2})$ complexity in the zero-noise regime. Numerical experiments on sparse phase retrieval, linear eigenvalue problems, and neural network regression show that all four ALFPG variants generally outperform state-of-the-art proximal-gradient baselines.
item.dc:creator: Ganzhao Yuan

item.title: Contractive kinetic Langevin samplers beyond global Lipschitz continuity
item.description: arXiv:2509.12031v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we examine the problem of sampling from log-concave distributions with (possibly) superlinear gradient growth under kinetic (underdamped) Langevin algorithms. Using a carefully tailored taming scheme, we propose two novel discretizations of the kinetic Langevin SDE, the tamed exponential euler scheme and tamed OBABO and we show that they are both contractive and satisfy a log-Sobolev inequality. Building on this, we establish a series of non-asymptotic bounds in $2$-Wasserstein and total variation distance between the law reached by each algorithm and the underlying target measure. In particular, we show that both algorithms can reach almost optimal $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-1})$ convergence rate in Wasserstein and Total Variation distances, and $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-\frac{1}{2}})$ under increased Hessian local regularity for the tamed OBABO scheme.
item.dc:creator: Iosif Lytras, Panayotis Mertikopoulos

item.title: Free Decompression with Algebraic Spectral Curves
item.description: arXiv:2605.03634v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tools from random matrix theory have become central to deep learning theory, using spectral information to provide mechanisms for modeling generalization, robustness, scaling, and failure modes. While often capable of modeling empirical behavior, practical computations are limited by matrix size, often imposing a restriction to models that are too small to be realistic. This motivates the inference of properties of larger models from the behavior of smaller ones. Free decompression (FD) is a recently proposed method for extrapolating spectral information across matrix sizes, but its utility is currently limited by strong assumptions that preclude its implementation on more realistic machine learning (ML) models. We use algebraic spectral curve theory to provide a general FD methodology for spectral densities whose Stieltjes transform satisfies an algebraic relation, a modeling assumption that is more likely to hold in practice. This recasts FD as an evolution along spectral curves which can be readily integrated. Our framework enables the expansion of spectral densities that have multiple or multi-modal bulks, that exist at multiple scales, and that contain atoms, all characteristic of real-world data and popular ML models. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework on models of interest in modern ML, including Hessian and activation matrices associated with neural networks and large-scale diffusion models.
item.dc:creator: Siavash Ameli, Chris van der Heide, Liam Hodgkinson, Michael W. Mahoney

item.title: Why Directly Learning Periodic Trajectories Can Fail
item.description: arXiv:2609.32254v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Operator learning of periodic solutions requires deciding how simulation data should be recorded and represented. A natural choice is to integrate long enough for transients to decay and record a window wide enough to contain at least one full period of all trajectories. We find that these conservative choices can make the resulting trajectories difficult to learn, even when the underlying periodic orbits vary regularly with system parameters. Unaligned trajectories generalize poorly even within the training distribution. Phase alignment substantially improves in-distribution generalization, but models trained on a fixed physical-time window still have large errors on trajectories with periods outside the training range. We explain both failures through a common mechanism: frequency differences accumulate over time, so the target phase varies rapidly with the parameters. Predictors that cannot track this variation incur a population MSE floor in both settings; for fixed window prediction, we also derive a per-sample lower bound. We then study one of the simplest representations that escape these floors: learning an aligned, normalized waveform and its period separately. We establish regularity of the decoupled targets under ODE assumptions and show experimentally that this approach avoids both failures in ODE systems and a PDE case study.
item.dc:creator: Kaixin Zheng, Anita Layton

item.title: AECSF: Adaptive Ensemble Conditional Score Filtering for High-Dimensional Nonlinear Data Assimilation
item.description: arXiv:2609.32411v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In high-dimensional filters, particle weights can concentrate on a few members, while Gaussian updates can miss non-Gaussian posterior structure. A diffusion filter updates a forecast ensemble by gradually denoising particles in light of a new observation. Each noisy particle can correspond to several system states, and these states can have very different likelihoods. A score correction based on a single state can therefore misrepresent the posterior. We propose the Adaptive Ensemble Conditional Score Filter (AECSF), which uses the conditional Tweedie identity to express the required score through the mean state given the particle and the observation. All reverse particles share a set of proposals, but each assigns its own weights to estimate its conditional mean. As denoising proceeds, the reverse particles guide which proposals are resampled. We characterize when fixed proposals yield the exact noisy posterior score and bound the contribution of conditional-mean errors to the final sampling error. In controlled Gaussian experiments, AECSF samples the posterior more accurately than the tested likelihood-guidance rules. With 20 forecast members in 10,000-dimensional Lorenz-96, AECSF has lower RMSE and CRPS than the tested tempered SMC and kernel-density filters. On Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, the analysis ensembles also improve subsequent forecasts over the tested baselines at comparable cost. For Navier-Stokes flow, we learn a forecast prior that captures spatial dependence in vorticity and use it to reconstruct the full field from sparse velocity measurements.
item.dc:creator: Yangwen Zhang, Shiwei Ni, Xiaoping Zhang, Xiaofei Guan, Lili Ju

item.title: Change the Number, Change the Answer: Assessing Rating Scale Sensitivity in LLM-Based Text Scoring
item.description: arXiv:2610.22187v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in computational social science to assign scalar scores to social and psychological constructs. However, studies use different rating scales, and whether their scores remain comparable across scale designs is understudied. To address this gap, we define and systematically investigate scale sensitivity, the variation in LLM-generated scores caused by rating scale design. We distinguish numerical sensitivity, changes in normalized scores, from semantic sensitivity, changes in score interpretation. To assess both, our experimental design crosses 2 formats (continuous vs. ordinal), 4 ranges (3, 5, 11, and 21 points), and 2 signs (signed vs. unsigned) across 3 tasks (political leaning, sentiment, and toxicity), 2 prompting strategies (zero-shot and rubric-based), and 5 LLMs. We find that changing one design element shifts normalized scores by about 0.10 on average and changes the category of roughly 20% of texts. Sensitivity is greatest for toxicity, the only unipolar construct examined. Also, rubric-based prompting does not reduce sensitivity compared with zero-shot prompting. We provide practical guidance for designing more reliable LLM-based text scoring and highlight the need for robustness checks across alternative scales.
item.dc:creator: Wonjeong Jo, Gyuwan Kim, Ming Shan Hee

item.title: Consistent interfacial flow numerics - Part II: The momentum convection term
item.description: arXiv:2611.24866v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The two-phase Volume-of-Fluid solvers of OpenFOAM overpredict the horizontal water velocity near the crest of a water wave, and the error grows as the wave propagates. Part I of this series removed the spurious air velocities caused by the gravity term but left this error unchanged. Here we show that it is caused by the momentum convection term. Its mass flux is computed in the interface advection step from the velocity at the start of the time step, whereas the convected velocity is taken at the end of the step, because convection is discretised implicitly. In a progressive wave, where the horizontal and vertical velocities are 90 degrees out of phase, this time lag produces an upward flux of horizontal momentum, proportional to the time step, which accumulates in a spurious current near the surface. The same mismatch makes the response to a force depend on the density at the wrong time level. Explicit convection removes the lag and makes the response consistent with the gravity force, but requires the convected face velocity at the interface to be taken from the upwind cell. Only then is the new velocity of a cell a weighted average of old velocities, whatever the density ratio. We demonstrate both requirements with prescribed flows and with the full solver. For a progressive wave, explicit convection with upwind face velocities at the interface reduces the overprediction of the crest velocity from 26-31 % to within 1 % and removes the near-surface current. The resulting solver, fluxinator, is meant for maximum Courant numbers of 0.1 and below, where it keeps the wave height within 1.5 % over 15 periods on meshes with six or more cells per wave height. Because the spurious velocities that limit the time step are removed, it needs 34-42 % less wall-clock time than interFoam for the tested wave.
item.dc:creator: Johan Roenby
